newsitem.title: USA: Clinton budget sees slower economic growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Clinton budget sees slower economic growth in 1997.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The Clinton administration said on Thursday that it expects economic growth to slow down, but not stop, in 1997 and forecast lower interest rates in the years ahead if the federal budget is balanced.
In its fiscal year 1998 budget proposal presented to Congress, the administration also said it expects inflation to moderate this year and the unemployment rate to tick up.

The economic forecasts form the bedrock of a proposed $1.69 trillion budget that aims to eliminate the deficit by the year 2002 while still providing the middle class with tax relief and protecting President Clinton's spending priorities.
The administration said it expects economic growth to slow down to a 2 percent pace both this year and next. On a fourth quarter on fourth quarter basis, the economy grew by 3.4 percent last year.
The forecast, which looks to have been compiled before news of a surge in growth at the end of last year, is basically in line with that of top private economists.
The administration though is somewhat more optimistic than private forecasters on the outlook for inflation.

It sees inflation slowing to 2.6 percent in 1997 from 3.1 percent in 1996, although part of that drop may be due to changes in the way the much-maligned consumer price index is calculated. Inflation ticks back up to 2.7 percent in 1998.

The unemployment rate, currently hovering around an eight-year low at 5.3 percent, is expected to rise to 5.4 percent in the fourth quarter of this year and 5.6 percent in the final three months of 1998, according to the budget.
The administration spent much of the economic portion of its budget proposal extolling the benefits of fiscal discipline and criticising the government's profligacy in the 1980s.
"Deficit cutting can go hand-in-hand with economic growth -- if the deficit cutting allows the Federal Reserve to maintain low interest rates and if it's credible with financial markets," it said.
It forecast lower short and long-term interest rates if the budget, which was in the red to the tune of $107.3 billion in the fiscal year that ended last Sept. 30, is balanced.
"A bipartisan agreement this year would greatly foster chances of further cuts in both short and long-term rates," the administration said.
The proposal apparently assumes no increase in short-term interest rates by the Federal Reserve this year, despite expectations to the contrary by many private experts.
The U.S. central bank decided on Wednesday to leave interest rates unchanged for the 12th straight month.
The budget expects the rate on three-month Treasury bills -- often seen as a proxy for the rates the Fed controls -- to hold steady at an average of 5 percent this year.
If the budget is balanced, the administration sees that rate gradually falling to 4 percent by 2001 and holding there. The three-month bill rate is now around 5.13 percent.

The administration also expects a gradual decline in long-term interest rates if the budget is balanced, with the yield on 10-year Treasury notes projected to fall gradually to 5.1 percent by the year 2001. It is now about 6.46 percent.
The administration defended its forecasts, which are slightly more optimistic on the whole than those of the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office, as sensible.

But the budget contains a provision to ensure that it reaches balance should the administration's forecasts prove too rosy. If that proves to be the case, the administration would repeal most of the budget's proposed tax cuts and levy an across-the-board reduction in spending.
